en: What could your wretched uncle do?
His cry reached God;
He fell, embracing the earth.
Into an opening in the yurt's lattice
Kobosh's head was thrust.
Before he could pull his head free,
Before he could regain his senses,
He struck him in the side with a kick;
Black blood flowed from his mouth,
Yellow bile flowed from his rear.
Then his uncle, Abyke—
Look at their wickedness!
Muttering and working himself up,
Speaking where Semetey could not hear,
To foolish Kobosh
He looked ready to lend support;
His wineskin-like face grew red,
Rising, rising again,
As he was about to rise,
About to lay hands on the child,
That fearsome madman Kobosh
Had not a glimmer of sense left.
Your champion Bakai held fast,
Not letting Abyke stand,
And spoke these precious words:
“Ah, dear Abyke, ah, dear one,
These fighting kinsmen will make peace.
If your orphan takes offense,
What will they say tomorrow?
Dear Abyke, be patient;
At patience's end lies yellow gold.
If you are patient, you will prosper;
If you are impatient, you will come to ruin!
Take care, Abyke:
If you side with Kobosh,
And I side with the child,
How could our shame be covered?
If we fail to restrain ourselves,
If we set to beating one another,
If we come to see hell,
Dust surges from a whirlwind,
Black blood flows from a quarrel,
And where blood goes, life goes.
If we commit such wickedness,
Dear Abyke, what happens afterward?
How can regret be dispelled,
Where can kinsmen be found?
Our ruddy faces will be soot,
These damned buttocks will be bared.
Kokcholok, whom I ride on patrol—
Though old, I still have my mount.
However far gone I may be,
I still have strength to match yours.
Dear Abyke, take care:
If drawn forth with a sideways pull,
If we fight, splattered red,
Terrible is the harm of battle.”
Pleading with Abyke,
Bakai Khan held him back;
His eyes reddened like fire,
Bakai Khan stood blazing.
He lost consciousness and sprawled,
Lay limp like a dead man.
Like one gone to Judgment Day,
If you saw the damned wretch's face,
The weapon's handle had left his hand,
The covering had left his heart.
His vigor fled, his strength was gone;
Black blood flowed from his chest.
His closed eyes would not open,
His outstretched leg would not draw back,
The blood from his chest would not stop.
Kobosh lay sprawled there,
For a meat-boiling's time, without recovering.
A grievous affliction had struck Kobosh;
Like one about to meet Judgment Day,
His wispy mustache drooped.
When mighty Manas died,
When the dogs divided the spoils,
Akkelte was taken as plunder;
Its defect was known.
Of your mountain-like uncle Kobosh,
Khan Manas's Akkelte—
When the child unleashed his wrath,
When Kobosh and this child
Set to pummeling one another,
And made a spectacle before the crowd,
The keen Kelte left by Manas,
Whose keenness the people had tested,
The support Manas had left,
Kicked against the yurt's lattice,
And banged away all by itself,
It boomed all by itself.
It roared all by itself,
It thundered all by itself.
If you ask of Akkelte's state,
It worked itself up,
It changed its aspect by itself.
Now he saw Akkelte;
Your orphan left by Manas,
Recognizing Kelte,
Hung it over his shoulder-blade.
Into the wealth denied when asked for
He now entered by force.
Looking toward the yurt's side,
Khan Manas's Syrnayza,
Drenched in black blood,
Its grip of golden gemstone—
He had diverse woods turned,
Had them glued with copper mixed in,
Made so they could not come apart.
He had it fashioned joint by joint;
Lest it slip from the hand,
He had it covered in elephant hide.
A handspan he had painted,
A handspan he had pared.
Its steel point, a wolf's tongue,
Would not turn back from stone;
He had it fitted from white steel,
Felling the enemy it fought.
The lame smith Bolokbay
Was a friend of David:
“May all whom it strikes
Sicken grievously and die,” he said,
And quenched it with human tears.
The mighty smith Bolokbay
Drew out all its iron,
Pounding it with his sledgehammer.
Unable to meet its need for charcoal,
The edge of the forest was hollowed away.
Unable to meet its need for bellows,
Many young bulls were slaughtered.
“A gift my father left,” he said,
And Semetey took that too.
“If I live and do not die,
I shall shout and thrust my lance,” he said.
“I shall give many a spectacle,” he said.
“I shall smash them and take revenge,” he said.
Semetey took Syrnayza;
And he had more to say:
“The six keen blades fallen from heaven,
The perfect treasure given by Allah,
Which devastated the land of the Chinese—
Never catching as they were swung,
When swung against the foe,
Their keenness killed.
Unless they had drunk their fill of blood,
They would not enter their sheaths when put away.
Unless they had seen a mighty slaughter,
They would not look back and go idle.
Those six heavenly blades,
This witless dog Kobosh
Has taken as plunder.
Without living by fighting enemies,
This swine of wicked ways,
Without dividing them among the companions,
Has gathered and taken them all.
Boz Kise and Akolpok—
Gathering everything together,
He tied them in Akolpok.
At the bottom of a great saddlebag,
He gathered and put them all.
Your stepmother Akylay—
Gathering up the great saddlebag,
She had laid it at her hip.
In great Kobosh's embrace
She lay and would not rise.
The witless wretch—
He swept that woman up and flung her,
Ah, the orphan child, the hero!
Akylay rolled away,
The wretch tumbled;
Rolling toward the stone hearth,
Akylay struck the ground.
Her back was bent and hunched;
She had no strength to utter “Ah,”
Her eyes bulged out.
Her knees ached, crushed and battered,
Every bone throbbed with pain.
“The humiliation I never suffered from Manas
I have suffered from his son,” she said,
Akylay weeping and shrieking.
The child prince, the orphan slave,
Appeared like a calamity.
The wealth that Manas left,
Without leaving so much as a hair,
From the hands of Abyke and Kobosh
He seemed to have seized.
Lifting the great saddlebag,
Semetey, onto Aktulpar,
Had apparently loaded it.
Making ready, full of spirit,
Preparing his weapons,
As the child was going out,
The support left by Manas,
That watchful Bakai,
To Manas's orphan son,
Biting his lip and winking,
As Bakai stood beside him,
Manas's son, the orphan hero—
The mighty treasure taken from China
Was in Abyke's hands.
What was there, and what was not!
Bukhara's costly yellow-mottled cloth,
Andijan's costly black-mottled weave,
Were packed in one saddlebag.
If you ask about that saddlebag,
Its lock was gold, its fastening copper,
Pale in color, measuring an arshin—
Now came this saddlebag's turn.
Satisfying the eye's desire,
Costly crimson fabric,
Mixed with gold and rubies,
Was packed in that saddlebag.
When the child took the saddlebag,
From his father, generous Manas,
The wealth that had remained—
Semetey had taken it, it seems.
Upon the six villains, terror
Semetey had brought, it seems.
Leaving none of his wealth behind,
Semetey had taken it, it seems.
Plundering their valuables thus,
Semetey had gone, it seems.
The six villains' ruin
Semetey had brought about, it seems.
This orphan of Manas,
An orphan, had grown to maturity,
And thus joined their ranks.
He grew to manhood, became a hero,
Became the equal of a hero's son.
Wherever your orphan arrived,
He raised turmoil among the six villains.
Manas's son, the rogue—
Even if he died, there was no regret.
In the hands of the six villains
Not a trace of anything remained.
Abyke stood there working himself up,
Speaking to the dog Kobosh.
“A fool has no kinsmen,
You care about nothing.
My fool, you have ruined me;
You meant to dig my pit,
You meant to boil my misery.
You meant to show my eyes
A wonder no human could bear to see.
You have proved a foolish villain;
My crimson-red treasures—
Unable to keep quiet without shouting,
My fool, you meant to ruin me.
Before you even saw the orphan,
You spoke to him of battle.
If you keep on like this, fool,
You will bring about my ruin.
Can a human be like you?
Can one who calls you human come to any good?
